claim: Pre-mRNA processing 4 (PRP4) kinase is a component of the U4/U5.U6 triple small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (tri-snRNP) spliceosome.
source: Through an RNA interference screen, we found that pre-mRNA processing 4 (PRP4) kinase, a component of the U4/U5.U6 triple small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (tri-snRNP) spliceosome, and other tri-snRNP components regulate cycling of the molecular clock as well as rest:activity rhythms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRP4's structural role in the spliceosome complex.

claim: PRP4 and other tri-snRNP components regulate cycling of the molecular clock.
source: Through an RNA interference screen, we found that pre-mRNA processing 4 (PRP4) kinase, a component of the U4/U5.U6 triple small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (tri-snRNP) spliceosome, and other tri-snRNP components regulate cycling of the molecular clock as well as rest:activity rhythms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA interference screen performed in the study.

claim: PRP4 and other tri-snRNP components regulate rest:activity rhythms.
source: Through an RNA interference screen, we found that pre-mRNA processing 4 (PRP4) kinase, a component of the U4/U5.U6 triple small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (tri-snRNP) spliceosome, and other tri-snRNP components regulate cycling of the molecular clock as well as rest:activity rhythms.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the RNA interference screen.

claim: Unbiased RNA-Sequencing uncovered an alternatively spliced intron in tim.
source: Unbiased RNA-Sequencing uncovered an alternatively spliced intron in tim whose increased retention upon prp4 downregulation leads to decreased TIM levels.
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased retention of an alternatively spliced intron in tim upon prp4 downregulation leads to decreased TIM levels.
source: Unbiased RNA-Sequencing uncovered an alternatively spliced intron in tim whose increased retention upon prp4 downregulation leads to decreased TIM levels.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data and protein level measurements in the study.

claim: The splicing of tim is rhythmic with a phase that parallels delayed accumulation of the protein in a 24 hr cycle.
source: We demonstrate that the splicing of tim is rhythmic with a phase that parallels delayed accumulation of the protein in a 24 hr cycle.
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR analysis of splicing across time points shown in Figure 6.

claim: Alternative splicing constitutes an important clock mechanism for delaying the daily accumulation of clock proteins.
source: We propose that alternative splicing constitutes an important clock mechanism for delaying the daily accumulation of clock proteins, and thereby negative feedback by them.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Alternative splicing delays negative feedback by clock proteins.
source: We propose that alternative splicing constitutes an important clock mechanism for delaying the daily accumulation of clock proteins, and thereby negative feedback by them.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed effects of splicing on protein accumulation and clock function.

claim: Circadian rhythms allow organisms to orchestrate behavioral and physiological outputs in anticipation of predictable diurnal changes in the environment.
source: Circadian rhythms allow organisms to orchestrate behavioral and physiological outputs in anticipation of predictable diurnal changes in the environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the circadian biology field.

claim: Circadian rhythms are generated by endogenous molecular clocks that entrain to environmental cycles, predominantly light and temperature.
source: These rhythms are generated by endogenous molecular clocks that entrain to environmental cycles, predominantly light and temperature, and can maintain rhythms when released into constant conditions (free-run).
evidence: This is established knowledge in circadian biology.

claim: Circadian clocks can maintain rhythms when released into constant conditions (free-run).
source: These rhythms are generated by endogenous molecular clocks that entrain to environmental cycles, predominantly light and temperature, and can maintain rhythms when released into constant conditions (free-run).
evidence: This is a fundamental property of circadian clocks established in the field.

claim: A conserved mechanistic feature of circadian clocks is an auto-regulatory transcriptional feedback loop in which circadian proteins rhythmically regulate their own expression.
source: A conserved mechanistic feature of circadian clocks is an auto-regulatory transcriptional feedback loop in which circadian proteins rhythmically regulate their own expression to generate a clock, and also drive a global program of cycling gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms.

claim: Circadian proteins drive a global program of cycling gene expression.
source: A conserved mechanistic feature of circadian clocks is an auto-regulatory transcriptional feedback loop in which circadian proteins rhythmically regulate their own expression to generate a clock, and also drive a global program of cycling gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock function.

claim: PERIOD (PER) and TIMELESS (TIM) are the auto-regulating elements of the circadian clock in Drosophila.
source: PERIOD (PER) and TIMELESS (TIM) are the auto-regulating elements of the circadian clock in Drosophila (Allada and Chung, 2010; Hardin, 2011; Zheng and Sehgal, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The expression of per and tim is driven by circadian transcription factors CLOCK (CLK) and CYCLE (CYC).
source: The expression of per and tim is driven by circadian transcription factors CLOCK (CLK) and CYCLE (CYC), and peaks around the early night.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila circadian clock mechanism.

claim: The expression of per and tim peaks around the early night.
source: The expression of per and tim is driven by circadian transcription factors CLOCK (CLK) and CYCLE (CYC), and peaks around the early night.
evidence: This is established knowledge about per and tim expression patterns.

claim: Accumulation of PER and TIM proteins is delayed by ~6 hr relative to their mRNA peak.
source: Relative to their mRNA peak, accumulation of PER and TIM proteins is delayed by ~6 hr.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the temporal dynamics of PER and TIM.

claim: In the mid-to-late night, PER and TIM are predominantly nuclear.
source: In the mid-to-late night, PER and TIM are predominantly nuclear, and once in the nucleus, they repress CLK-CYC activity to decrease per and tim expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PER and TIM localization and function.

claim: Once in the nucleus, PER and TIM repress CLK-CYC activity to decrease per and tim expression.
source: In the mid-to-late night, PER and TIM are predominantly nuclear, and once in the nucleus, they repress CLK-CYC activity to decrease per and tim expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the negative feedback mechanism.

claim: Degradation of TIM and then of PER in the morning resets the transcription cycle and restarts the loop.
source: Degradation of TIM and then of PER in the morning resets the transcription cycle and restarts the loop.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circadian clock reset mechanism.

claim: A stable circadian molecular oscillator requires temporal delays to separate the phases of gene transcription and repression.
source: In order to maintain rhythmicity and set the proper pace of the circadian clock, both PER and TIM need to be dynamically regulated on multiple levels. For instance, a stable circadian molecular oscillator requires temporal delays to separate the phases of gene transcription and repression and thereby prevent these from reaching equilibrium (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Temporal delays prevent gene transcription and repression from reaching equilibrium in the circadian clock.
source: For instance, a stable circadian molecular oscillator requires temporal delays to separate the phases of gene transcription and repression and thereby prevent these from reaching equilibrium (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: PER is the more important factor for transcriptional regulation compared to TIM.
source: Although PER is the more important factor for transcriptional regulation, levels and activity of PER depend upon TIM (Price et al., 1995; Dubruille and Emery, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Levels and activity of PER depend upon TIM.
source: Although PER is the more important factor for transcriptional regulation, levels and activity of PER depend upon TIM (Price et al., 1995; Dubruille and Emery, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Light promotes the degradation of TIM during the day.
source: TIM levels are acutely modulated by light, which promotes the degradation of TIM, and thereby PER, during the day and allows the rise in circadian transcription (Suri et al., 1999; Yang and Sehgal, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Light promotes the degradation of PER during the day through TIM degradation.
source: TIM levels are acutely modulated by light, which promotes the degradation of TIM, and thereby PER, during the day and allows the rise in circadian transcription (Suri et al., 1999; Yang and Sehgal, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Light-induced TIM degradation allows the rise in circadian transcription.
source: TIM levels are acutely modulated by light, which promotes the degradation of TIM, and thereby PER, during the day and allows the rise in circadian transcription (Suri et al., 1999; Yang and Sehgal, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: TIM accumulation is necessary to stabilize PER.
source: Subsequently, TIM accumulation is necessary to stabilize PER and promote its nuclear accumulation (Jang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: TIM accumulation promotes nuclear accumulation of PER.
source: Subsequently, TIM accumulation is necessary to stabilize PER and promote its nuclear accumulation (Jang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: In the presence of light:dark cycles, light delays the accumulation of TIM-PER and contributes to the lag in repression.
source: Thus, in the presence of light:dark cycles, light delays the accumulation of TIM-PER and so contributes to the lag in repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the established effects of light on TIM degradation.

claim: Temporal relationships between TIM and PER are largely preserved in constant darkness.
source: These temporal relationships are largely preserved in constant darkness, and are also entrained by temperature cycles regardless of light cues, although the mechanisms under these conditions are not known.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock behavior in different conditions.

claim: Temporal relationships between TIM and PER are entrained by temperature cycles regardless of light cues.
source: These temporal relationships are largely preserved in constant darkness, and are also entrained by temperature cycles regardless of light cues, although the mechanisms under these conditions are not known.
evidence: This is established knowledge about temperature entrainment of the clock.

claim: The mechanisms by which temporal relationships between TIM and PER are maintained in constant darkness and temperature cycles are not known.
source: These temporal relationships are largely preserved in constant darkness, and are also entrained by temperature cycles regardless of light cues, although the mechanisms under these conditions are not known.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Regulated protein stability and translation have been directly explored as mechanisms that could contribute to maintenance of the feedback loop.
source: While regulated protein stability and translation have been directly explored as mechanisms that could contribute to maintenance of the feedback loop (Dembinska et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1998 ;Lim and Allada, 2013; Zhang et al., 2013), and regulation of protein stability is indeed critical (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012), little investigation has focused on a potential role of alternative splicing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regulation of protein stability is critical for the circadian feedback loop.
source: While regulated protein stability and translation have been directly explored as mechanisms that could contribute to maintenance of the feedback loop (Dembinska et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1998 ;Lim and Allada, 2013; Zhang et al., 2013), and regulation of protein stability is indeed critical (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012), little investigation has focused on a potential role of alternative splicing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Little investigation has focused on a potential role of alternative splicing in the circadian feedback loop.
source: While regulated protein stability and translation have been directly explored as mechanisms that could contribute to maintenance of the feedback loop (Dembinska et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1998 ;Lim and Allada, 2013; Zhang et al., 2013), and regulation of protein stability is indeed critical (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012), little investigation has focused on a potential role of alternative splicing.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: The best-studied role for alternative splicing in Drosophila rhythms is in the temperature-dependence of the behavioral siesta.
source: To date, the best-studied role for alternative splicing in Drosophila rhythms is in the temperature-dependence of the behavioral siesta (Majercak et al., 1999; Majercak et al., 2004; Collins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Splicing is driven by spliceosomes, dynamic RNA-protein complexes composed of five core small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNP) and >150 additional proteins.
source: Splicing is driven by spliceosomes, dynamic RNA-protein complexes composed of five core small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNP) and >150 additional proteins specific for each snRNP complex (Wahl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spliceosome structure, supported by citation.

claim: PRP4 is a conserved component of the spliceosomal U4/U6.U5 triple small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (tri-snRNP) complex.
source: In this study, we report a circadian role for Pre-mRNA Processing factor 4 (PRP4), a conserved component of the spliceosomal U4/U6.U5 triple small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (tri-snRNP) complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRP4's structural role.

claim: PRP4 was identified in a screen for novel regulators of the free-running circadian period.
source: We identified PRP4 in a screen for novel regulators of the free-running circadian period, and established that PRP4 is necessary in tim+ clock cells to maintain 24 hr period and robust rhythms of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is supported by the screening data presented in the study.

claim: PRP4 is necessary in tim+ clock cells to maintain 24 hr period.
source: We identified PRP4 in a screen for novel regulators of the free-running circadian period, and established that PRP4 is necessary in tim+ clock cells to maintain 24 hr period and robust rhythms of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral and molecular data in the study.

claim: PRP4 is necessary in tim+ clock cells to maintain robust rhythms of the circadian clock.
source: We identified PRP4 in a screen for novel regulators of the free-running circadian period, and established that PRP4 is necessary in tim+ clock cells to maintain 24 hr period and robust rhythms of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing rhythm strength changes.

claim: Downregulation of multiple tri-snRNP components affected circadian period length and rhythmicity.
source: In addition to prp4, downregulation of multiple tri-snRNP components affected circadian period length and rhythmicity, which led us to implicate this entire spliceosomal complex in circadian regulation.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from RNAi experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: The entire tri-snRNP spliceosomal complex is implicated in circadian regulation.
source: In addition to prp4, downregulation of multiple tri-snRNP components affected circadian period length and rhythmicity, which led us to implicate this entire spliceosomal complex in circadian regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent effects of multiple tri-snRNP component knockdowns.

claim: A novel intron retention event in tim was identified using unbiased RNA-Sequencing.
source: Using unbiased RNA-Sequencing, we characterized the splicing events regulated by PRP4 and identified a novel intron retention event in tim.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Alternative splicing of an intron in tim represents an important mechanism to time the daily accumulation of TIM in constant darkness following entrainment to light:dark cycles.
source: We show that alternative splicing of this intron in tim represents an important mechanism to time the daily accumulation of TIM, in constant darkness following entrainment to light:dark cycles and also in temperature cycles.
evidence: This is supported by splicing and protein level data across time points in different conditions.

claim: Alternative splicing of an intron in tim represents an important mechanism to time the daily accumulation of TIM in temperature cycles.
source: We show that alternative splicing of this intron in tim represents an important mechanism to time the daily accumulation of TIM, in constant darkness following entrainment to light:dark cycles and also in temperature cycles.
evidence: This is supported by splicing data in temperature cycles shown in Figure 6.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of prp4 in tim+ clock neurons with the Tim-UAS-Gal4 (TUG) Gal4 driver resulted in consistently long free-running circadian periods.
source: RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated knockdown of prp4 in tim+ clock neurons with the Tim-UAS-Gal4 (TUG) Gal4 driver resulted in consistently long free-running circadian periods (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Two independent RNAi lines (GD and KK) were used to confirm the period lengthening effect of prp4 knockdown.
source: Two independent RNAi lines (GD and KK) were used to confirm these findings.
evidence: This is supported by data from both RNAi lines shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Flies with circadian-cell-specific prp4 knockdown exhibited a delayed evening activity peak in LD conditions.
source: Compared to controls, the flies with circadian-cell-specific prp4 knockdown (TUG; Dcr2 >prp4RNAi(GD)) exhibited a delayed evening activity peak as well as a slightly delayed morning peak.
evidence: This is supported by activity profile data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flies with circadian-cell-specific prp4 knockdown exhibited a slightly delayed morning peak in LD conditions.
source: Compared to controls, the flies with circadian-cell-specific prp4 knockdown (TUG; Dcr2 >prp4RNAi(GD)) exhibited a delayed evening activity peak as well as a slightly delayed morning peak.
evidence: This is supported by activity profile data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The delayed activity peaks in prp4 knockdown flies are consistent with the longer endogenous period.
source: These findings are consistent with the longer endogenous period that we report for prp4 knockdown flies (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the LD behavior to the free-running period data.

claim: The small lateral ventral neurons (s-LNvs) are the most relevant clock cells for driving rest:activity rhythms under constant dark conditions.
source: As the small lateral ventral neurons (s-LNvs) are the most relevant clock cells for driving rest:activity rhythms under constant dark conditions, we asked if effects of PRP4 were mediated in these cells (Helfrich-Förster, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Knockdown of prp4 with pdf-Gal4 driving the weaker RNAi line (GD) led to a modest yet significant lengthening of free-running circadian period.
source: Knockdown of prp4 with pdf-Gal4 driving the weaker RNAi line (GD) led to a modest yet significant lengthening of free-running circadian period (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Knockdown of prp4 with a stronger RNAi (KK) using pdf-Gal4 led to complex rhythms.
source: Interestingly, the knockdown of prp4 with a stronger RNAi (KK) led to complex rhythms (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Complex rhythms from strong prp4 knockdown were generally characterized by changes in the behavioral pattern, often manifest as phase shifts during day 4 or 5 of constant darkness.
source: These complex rhythms were generally characterized by changes in the behavioral pattern, often manifest as phase shifts during day 4 or 5 of constant darkness (see ~6 hr shift in the record shown), in the midst of an otherwise rhythmic record (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by representative activity records shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Complex rhythm phenotype could reflect uncoupling of period into two components of pdf+ and pdf- cell oscillators.
source: Such a complex rhythm phenotype could reflect uncoupling of period into two components of pdf+ and pdf- cell oscillators (Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PRP4 action in LNvs contributes to maintaining clock function.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that PRP4 action in LNvs contributes to maintaining clock function.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral effects of prp4 knockdown in LNvs.

claim: Cycling of both PER and TIM was affected in s-LNvs upon prp4 knockdown with the clock-specific TUG driver.
source: Cycling of both PER and TIM was affected in s-LNvs upon prp4 knockdown with the clock-specific TUG driver (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Total TIM levels were decreased during the night in s-LNvs upon prp4 knockdown.
source: Total TIM levels, as quantified by corrected total cell fluorescence (CTCF) image analysis, were decreased during the night (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantified immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: PER levels were lower in the late night (ZT20) in prp4 knockdown flies.
source: PER levels were also lower in the late night (ZT20), and especially so in the early morning (ZT2), in prp4 knockdown flies (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: PER levels were especially lower in the early morning (ZT2) in prp4 knockdown flies.
source: PER levels were also lower in the late night (ZT20), and especially so in the early morning (ZT2), in prp4 knockdown flies (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of PER was delayed beyond ~ZT20 upon prp4 knockdown.
source: Additionally, nuclear accumulation of PER was delayed beyond ~ZT20, the time point at which PER was already partially localized to the nucleus in control flies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The nuclear accumulation of PER was slower in flies with decreased prp4 (both GD and KK RNAi lines) than in controls at ZT18-ZT22.
source: We found that the nuclear accumulation of PER was slower in flies with decreased prp4 (both GD and KK RNAi lines) than in controls (TUG; Dcr2/+) at these time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by nuclear/total PER ratio data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TIM is necessary for nuclear accumulation of PER.
source: Because TIM is necessary for nuclear accumulation of PER (Vosshall et al., 1994; Saez and Young, 1996; Jang et al., 2015), reduced TIM accumulation could account for the delay and overall reduced nuclear expression of PER in s-LNvs (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which together could account for the longer free-running period.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Reduced TIM accumulation could account for the delay and overall reduced nuclear expression of PER in s-LNvs upon prp4 knockdown.
source: Because TIM is necessary for nuclear accumulation of PER (Vosshall et al., 1994; Saez and Young, 1996; Jang et al., 2015), reduced TIM accumulation could account for the delay and overall reduced nuclear expression of PER in s-LNvs (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which together could account for the longer free-running period.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed TIM and PER phenotypes.

claim: Reduced TIM accumulation and delayed nuclear PER expression together could account for the longer free-running period upon prp4 knockdown.
source: Because TIM is necessary for nuclear accumulation of PER (Vosshall et al., 1994; Saez and Young, 1996; Jang et al., 2015), reduced TIM accumulation could account for the delay and overall reduced nuclear expression of PER in s-LNvs (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which together could account for the longer free-running period.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular and behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of prp4 consistently resulted in ~50% reduction in prp4 RNA in head lysates.
source: We consistently observed ~50% reduction in prp4 RNA in head lysates of flies where it was knocked down pan-neuronally (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pan-neuronal prp4 downregulation had a strong effect on total TIM levels, particularly during the initial TIM accumulation phase (ZT10-18).
source: First, we observed a strong effect of prp4 downregulation on total TIM levels, particularly during the initial TIM accumulation phase (ZT10-18) (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: prp4 knockdown blunted the circadian cycling of TIM protein.
source: Quantification of our western blot data across multiple experiments suggested that prp4 knockdown also blunted the circadian cycling of TIM protein (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantified western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The total levels of PER were not changed upon prp4 downregulation.
source: While the total levels of PER were not changed upon prp4 downregulation, its phosphorylation profile was dampened.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The phosphorylation profile of PER was dampened upon prp4 downregulation.
source: While the total levels of PER were not changed upon prp4 downregulation, its phosphorylation profile was dampened.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing altered PER migration patterns in Figure 2D.

claim: In control flies, PER was increasingly phosphorylated in the late night and early morning up until its degradation.
source: In control (elavGal4; Dcr2/+) flies, as previously reported (Edery et al., 1994), PER was increasingly phosphorylated in the late night and early morning up until its degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and confirmed by western blot data.

claim: In flies with reduced prp4 levels, PER migrated at a lower molecular weight on western blots (ZT18-ZT2).
source: In flies with reduced prp4 levels, PER migrated at a lower molecular weight on western blots (ZT18-ZT2).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dampened phosphorylation profile of PER upon prp4 depletion could reflect the defect in nuclear accumulation of PER because a number of sites on PER get phosphorylated only when PER starts to accumulate in the nucleus (after ZT20).
source: We speculate that the dampened phosphorylation profile of PER reflects, at least in part, the defect in nuclear accumulation of PER because a number of sites on PER get phosphorylated only when PER starts to accumulate in the nucleus (after ZT20) (Chiu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge about PER phosphorylation, supported by citation.

claim: prp4 depletion could have a TIM-independent effect on PER to regulate its phosphorylation profile.
source: Alternatively, prp4 depletion could have a TIM-independent effect on PER to regulate its phosphorylation profile.
evidence: This is an alternative speculation about the mechanism.

claim: PRP4 is associated with kinase activity.
source: As noted above, PRP4 is associated with kinase activity, but it is also a component of the spliceosome (Kojima et al., 2001; Schneider et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior.
source: Strikingly, clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) and pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31), which are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP, as well as pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) and bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2), which are associated with U5 snRNP, caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1.

claim: Clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31) caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior.
source: Strikingly, clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) and pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31), which are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP, as well as pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) and bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2), which are associated with U5 snRNP, caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1.

claim: Clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior.
source: Strikingly, clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) and pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31), which are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP, as well as pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) and bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2), which are associated with U5 snRNP, caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1.

claim: Clock-specific downregulation of bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2) caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior.
source: Strikingly, clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) and pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31), which are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP, as well as pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) and bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2), which are associated with U5 snRNP, caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1.

claim: prp3 and prp31 are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP.
source: Strikingly, clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) and pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31), which are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP, as well as pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) and bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2), which are associated with U5 snRNP, caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spliceosome component associations.

claim: prp8 and brr2 are associated with U5 snRNP.
source: Strikingly, clock-specific downregulation of pre-mRNA processing factor 3 (prp3) and pre-mRNA processing factor 31 (prp31), which are associated primarily with U4/U6 snRNP, as well as pre-mRNA processing factor 8 (prp8) and bad response to refrigeration 2 (brr2), which are associated with U5 snRNP, caused pronounced defects in free-running circadian behavior (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spliceosome component associations.

claim: The phenotypes from tri-snRNP component knockdown ranged from period lengthening to complete arrhythmicity.
source: The phenotypes ranged from period lengthening to complete arrhythmicity, suggesting that the overall levels and/or stability of tri-snRNP regulate circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is supported by the range of behavioral phenotypes shown in Table 1.

claim: The overall levels and/or stability of tri-snRNP regulate circadian rhythms.
source: The phenotypes ranged from period lengthening to complete arrhythmicity, suggesting that the overall levels and/or stability of tri-snRNP regulate circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent effects of multiple tri-snRNP component knockdowns.

claim: The s-LNvs of flies with downregulated prp8 had lower TIM levels at night.
source: We found that the s-LNvs of flies with downregulated prp8 had lower TIM levels at night, and also showed decreased nuclear accumulation at ZT20 relative to control flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The s-LNvs of flies with downregulated prp8 showed decreased nuclear accumulation at ZT20 relative to control flies.
source: We found that the s-LNvs of flies with downregulated prp8 had lower TIM levels at night, and also showed decreased nuclear accumulation at ZT20 relative to control flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Circadian oscillations of TIM are sensitive to changes in the levels of multiple tri-snRNP components.
source: These data allow us to conclude that circadian oscillations of PER (data not shown) and TIM are sensitive to changes in the levels of multiple tri-snRNP components.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent TIM phenotypes with different tri-snRNP component knockdowns.

claim: The heterozygous prp8/+ and brr2/+ mutants displayed normal circadian rhythms.
source: The heterozygous prp8/+ and brr2/+ mutants displayed normal circadian rhythms, readily explained by the haplosufficiency of these two genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: prp8 and brr2 are haploinsufficient genes.
source: The heterozygous prp8/+ and brr2/+ mutants displayed normal circadian rhythms, readily explained by the haplosufficiency of these two genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the normal rhythms in heterozygous mutants.

claim: Transheterozygous prp8/brr2 mutant flies had normal circadian period.
source: Transheterozygous prp8/brr2 mutant flies had normal circadian period (data not shown), but displayed decreased rhythm strength compared to the prp8/+ and brr2/+ heterozygous flies, confirming a circadian function of the tri-snRNP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Transheterozygous prp8/brr2 mutant flies displayed decreased rhythm strength compared to the prp8/+ and brr2/+ heterozygous flies.
source: Transheterozygous prp8/brr2 mutant flies had normal circadian period (data not shown), but displayed decreased rhythm strength compared to the prp8/+ and brr2/+ heterozygous flies, confirming a circadian function of the tri-snRNP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The decreased rhythm strength in transheterozygous prp8/brr2 mutants confirms a circadian function of the tri-snRNP.
source: Transheterozygous prp8/brr2 mutant flies had normal circadian period (data not shown), but displayed decreased rhythm strength compared to the prp8/+ and brr2/+ heterozygous flies, confirming a circadian function of the tri-snRNP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction between prp8 and brr2.

claim: Analysis of clock transcripts indicated an increase in tim levels in the late night in flies with reduced prp4.
source: Analysis of clock transcripts indicated an increase in tim levels in the late night in flies with reduced prp4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but in order to apply an unbiased approach, we performed RNA-Sequencing (RNA-Seq) analysis of fly heads in which prp4 had been knocked down.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overall gene expression was dramatically influenced by prp4 downregulation (433 down, 310 up at FDR < 0.05).
source: Overall gene expression was dramatically influenced by prp4 downregulation (433 down, 310 up at FDR < 0.05) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis identified changes in folate biosynthesis upon prp4 downregulation.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis using DAVID identified changes in folate biosynthesis as well as in other broad pathway categories such as protein export, protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum and drug metabolism (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by DAVID pathway analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Components of folate metabolism have been previously implicated in circadian clock regulation in human cells.
source: Interestingly, components of folate metabolism have been previously implicated in circadian clock regulation in human cells (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Despite PRP4 being a component of the core spliceosome required for constitutive splicing, dramatic effects on global splicing were not detected upon prp4 downregulation.
source: Despite the fact that PRP4 is a component of the core spliceosome required for constitutive splicing, we did not detect dramatic effects on global splicing.
evidence: This is supported by the limited number of differentially spliced genes identified in RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: 45 genes exhibited differential splicing upon prp4 downregulation, with FDR ≤ 0.05.
source: Using the Comprehensive AS Hunting (CASH) method, which assays for splicing events, our analysis identified 45 genes exhibiting differential splicing upon prp4 downregulation, with FDR ≤ 0.05 (Wu, W., et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by CASH analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: An intron retention event in tim was significantly upregulated upon prp4 knockdown.
source: An intron retention event in tim that was significantly upregulated upon prp4 knockdown was of particular interest due to its potential clock function (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq splicing analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The same retention event in tim (tim-tiny) was consistently identified as significantly upregulated with both CASH and Cufflinks analyses.
source: Importantly, the same retention event in tim, at position chr2L:3499764–3500000 (hereafter we refer to this intron as tim-tiny for simplicity), was consistently identified as significantly upregulated with both analyses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by convergent results from two independent analysis methods.

claim: Differential alternative splicing in only four other genes (trol, pex7, Npc1a, vsg) was consistently identified with both CASH and Cufflinks algorithms.
source: For comparison, differential alternative splicing in only four other genes (trol, pex7, Npc1a, vsg) was consistently identified with both of the algorithms (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of results from two analysis methods shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The RNA-Seq reads across the tim-tiny junction normalized to its neighboring junction were significantly increased in the prp4 knockdown samples compared to the controls.
source: Moreover, the RNA-Seq reads across the tiny-tiny junction normalized to its neighboring junction (2L:3500362–3500422), which is spliced out in all of the tim isoforms, were significantly increased in the prp4 knockdown samples (GMR >prp4RNAi) compared to the controls (GMR/+), further pointing to the retention of tim-tiny.
evidence: This is supported by normalized RNA-Seq read counts shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The isoforms retaining tim-tiny were twice as abundant as other isoforms at ZT 8 in control flies.
source: This analysis indicated that the isoforms retaining tim-tiny were twice as abundant as other isoforms at ZT 8 (when all of the RNA-Seq samples were collected) (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by Cufflinks quantification of isoform abundance.

claim: Increased tim-tiny retention was consistently detected upon pan-neuronal prp4 knockdown using qPCR.
source: Using this approach, increased tim-tiny retention was consistently detected upon pan-neuronal prp4 knockdown (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR validation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Intron inclusion in tim had a drastic effect on the total levels of TIM in S2 cells, ranging from highest when no intron was present to no detectable full size TIM when splicing was blocked with a mutation.
source: Intron inclusion had a drastic effect on the total levels of TIM, ranging from highest in the condition when no intron was present to no detectable full size TIM in the condition when splicing was blocked with the mutation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from S2 cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of the tim construct with the 5' splice site mutation led to low level production of a shorter TIM isoform called TIMtiny.
source: Expression of the construct with the 5' splice site mutation led to low level production of a shorter TIM isoform that we called TIMtiny.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from S2 cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TIMtiny was entirely absent when tim cDNA lacking the tim-tiny intron was expressed.
source: This isoform was entirely absent when tim cDNA lacking the tim-tiny intron was expressed but was produced upon expression of the cDNA construct that included tim-tiny.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from S2 cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TIMtiny is a truncated TIM isoform generated from the tim mRNA carrying an unspliced tim-tiny intron.
source: Therefore, TIMtiny is a truncated TIM isoform generated from the tim mRNA carrying an unspliced tim-tiny intron.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns of different tim constructs.

claim: Total mRNA levels were not different between the three tim cDNA experimental conditions in S2 cells.
source: Total mRNA levels were not different between these three experimental conditions, pointing to the post-transcriptional regulation of TIM protein abundance (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: tim-tiny retention regulates TIM protein abundance at the post-transcriptional level.
source: Total mRNA levels were not different between these three experimental conditions, pointing to the post-transcriptional regulation of TIM protein abundance (data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mRNA levels don't change but protein levels do.

claim: Overexpression of tim using the Gal4-UAS system reduces rhythmicity and increases free-running periods.
source: Normally, overexpression of tim using the Gal4-UAS system reduces rhythmicity and increases free-running periods, likely due to prolonged expression of the excess protein coupled with little negative feedback to downregulate production (Yang and Sehgal, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of 'tim-spliced' and 'tim-retained' cDNAs caused lengthening of free-running periods.
source: Overexpression of 'tim-spliced' and 'tim-retained' cDNAs caused lengthening of free-running periods (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The circadian behavior of flies overexpressing the cDNA construct with the 5' splice site mutation in tim-tiny was not different from that of the controls.
source: However, the circadian behavior of flies overexpressing the cDNA construct with the 5' splice site mutation in tim-tiny (TUG; Dcr2 > tim-retained + ssM) was not different from that of the controls (TUG; Dcr2/+).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Flies that overexpressed 'tim-retained-ssM' cDNA did not have increased TIMfull relative to controls.
source: As predicted, flies that overexpressed 'tim-retained-ssM' cDNA did not have increased TIMfull relative to controls, although both 'tim-spliced' and 'tim-retained' transgenes expressed abundant amounts of protein.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A band likely corresponding to TIMtiny was detected in flies overexpressing 'tim-retained-ssM' cDNA, which was absent in controls.
source: Interestingly, we detected a band, likely corresponding to TIMtiny, in TUG; Dcr2 > tim-retained + ssM flies, which was absent in the TUG; Dcr2/+ controls.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Selective tim-tiny retention acts to reduce overall TIM levels.
source: These data further corroborate our S2 cell findings and suggest that selective tim-tiny retention acts to reduce overall TIM levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined S2 cell and fly data.

claim: Expression of tim cDNA with a 5' splice site mutation in tim-tiny did not restore rhythms in tim0 flies.
source: As expected, the expression of tim cDNA with a 5' splice site mutation in tim-tiny ('tim-retained + ssM') did not restore rhythms in tim0 flies (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 'tim-retained' and 'tim-spliced' cDNA constructs rescued rhythms in 54% and 32% of tim0 flies, respectively.
source: The other two cDNA constructs, 'tim-retained' and 'tim-spliced' rescued rhythms in 54% and 32% of tim0 flies, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There was a significant difference in period length between tim0 flies rescued with 'tim-retained' versus 'tim-spliced' constructs.
source: Importantly, there was a significant difference in period length between the flies that were rhythmic (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by period analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The 'tim-retained' isoform rescued tim0 flies with periods of approximately 26 hr.
source: As discussed above, the UAS-GAL4 system typically over-expresses proteins and so rescues per/tim mutants with longer periods (Yang and Sehgal, 2001), which we observed for the 'tim-retained' isoform (~26 hr).
evidence: This is supported by period data shown in Figure 5F and established knowledge.

claim: Shorter periods were seen with the 'tim-spliced' version in tim0 rescue experiments.
source: Shorter periods were seen with the 'tim-spliced' version (Figure 5F), supporting the idea that tim-tiny retention promotes clock delays.
evidence: This is supported by period data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: tim-tiny retention promotes clock delays.
source: Shorter periods were seen with the 'tim-spliced' version (Figure 5F), supporting the idea that tim-tiny retention promotes clock delays.
evidence: This is inferred from the period differences between rescue constructs.

claim: In LD conditions, intron retention of tim-tiny did not display a significant cycle by JTK analysis but showed a peak at ZT8.
source: In LD conditions, intron retention of tim-tiny did not display a significant cycle (by JTK analysis) but nevertheless showed a peak at ZT8.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In DD conditions, robust cycling of tim-tiny was observed with a crest at CT8.
source: In DD conditions, interestingly, we observed robust cycling of tim-tiny with a crest at CT8.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: tim-cold intron retention cycled in both LD and DD with similar phases, with peak intron retention during the day in LD and the subjective day in DD.
source: We found that tim-cold retention cycled in both LD and DD with similar phases, such that peak intron retention was during the day in LD and the subjective day in DD.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: In per01 flies under both LD and DD conditions, the cycling of both tim-tiny and tim-cold intron retention was abolished.
source: In per01 flies under both LD and DD conditions, the cycling of both tim-tiny and tim-cold intron retention was abolished, indicating that the circadian clock drives circadian oscillations in tim splicing.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data in per01 mutants shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The circadian clock drives circadian oscillations in tim splicing.
source: In per01 flies under both LD and DD conditions, the cycling of both tim-tiny and tim-cold intron retention was abolished, indicating that the circadian clock drives circadian oscillations in tim splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of splicing rhythms in clock mutants.

claim: Retention of the tim-tiny intron during the day serves to delay the accumulation of TIM protein, particularly when light is not available to degrade TIM.
source: We suggest that retention of the tim-tiny intron during the day serves to delay the accumulation of TIM protein, in particular when light is not available to degrade TIM.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the splicing and protein data.

claim: tim-cold retention is regulated by temperature and peaks at colder temperatures.
source: It was previously reported that tim-cold retention is regulated by temperature and peaks at colder temperatures (Boothroyd et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Temperature cycles were able to drive tim expression in constant dark.
source: In constant dark, temperature cycles were able to drive tim expression as previously reported (Glaser, F.T., and Stanewsky, R., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and confirmed by data in Figure 6C.

claim: The profile of tim-cold retention was cyclic with the highest retention levels during the colder (25°C) temperatures in temperature cycles in constant dark.
source: Additionally, the profile of tim-cold retention was cyclic with the highest retention levels during the colder (25°C) temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data in temperature cycles shown in Figure 6C.

claim: tim-tiny retention was robustly rhythmic under temperature cycles in constant dark, with increased retention at higher temperatures and decreased retention at lower temperatures.
source: Interestingly, tim-tiny retention was robustly rhythmic under these temperature conditions, yet, unlike tim-cold, intron retention was increased by higher temperatures and decreased by lower ones.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data in temperature cycles shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Higher temperatures, which are typically associated with daytime hours, may reduce TIM levels by regulating the splicing of tim-tiny.
source: Thus, higher temperatures, which are typically associated with daytime hours, may reduce TIM levels by regulating the splicing of tim-tiny, while light does so through TIM degradation (Hunter-Ensor et al., 1996; Myers et al., 1996; Zeng et al., 1996; Naidoo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the temperature-dependent splicing data.

claim: Light reduces TIM levels through TIM degradation.
source: Thus, higher temperatures, which are typically associated with daytime hours, may reduce TIM levels by regulating the splicing of tim-tiny, while light does so through TIM degradation (Hunter-Ensor et al., 1996; Myers et al., 1996; Zeng et al., 1996; Naidoo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: More robust cycling of tim-tiny was observed under temperature cycles in constant light conditions.
source: We observed the same relationship and even more robust cycling of tim-tiny under temperature cycles (12 hr:12 hr 30°C:25°C) in constant light conditions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: tim-cold did not cycle under temperature cycles in constant light conditions.
source: In these conditions, tim-cold did not cycle, further indicating different regulation of these two splicing events in tim.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: tim-tiny and tim-cold splicing events are regulated differently.
source: In these conditions, tim-cold did not cycle, further indicating different regulation of these two splicing events in tim.
evidence: This is inferred from the different responses to temperature cycles in constant light.

claim: The circadian profile of tim-tiny intron retention (high during the daytime) is consistent with it delaying the accumulation of TIM protein.
source: The circadian profile of tim-tiny intron retention (i.e. high during the daytime) is consistent with it delaying the accumulation of TIM protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between splicing and protein accumulation.

claim: The tim-tiny splicing mechanism is particularly robust in DD and in temperature cycles in constant light conditions.
source: Indeed, this mechanism is particularly robust in DD (Figure 6) and also in temperature cycles in constant light conditions (Glaser and Stanewsky, 2005; Yoshii et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by splicing data in different conditions shown in Figure 6.

claim: The retention of tim-tiny peaks at high temperatures, which correlates with low TIM levels.
source: The retention of tim-tiny peaks at high temperatures, which correlates with low TIM levels (Glaser, F.T., and Stanewsky, R., 2005; Yoshii et al., 2005).
evidence: This correlation is supported by the current splicing data and cited literature on TIM levels.

claim: The splice choice at the tim-tiny locus modulates the rate of TIM accumulation.
source: We propose a model (Figure 7) whereby the splice choice at the tim-tiny locus modulates the rate of TIM accumulation, which in turn affects the total levels of nuclear PER and TIM.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The splice choice at the tim-tiny locus affects the total levels of nuclear PER and TIM.
source: We propose a model (Figure 7) whereby the splice choice at the tim-tiny locus modulates the rate of TIM accumulation, which in turn affects the total levels of nuclear PER and TIM.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The intron retention of tim-tiny likely contributes to a delay between initial tim expression and accumulation of TIM, ensuring stability and robustness of the circadian oscillator.
source: The intron retention of tim-tiny, therefore, likely contributes to a delay between initial tim expression and accumulation of TIM, ensuring stability and robustness of the circadian oscillator.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: The response of tim-tiny splicing to temperature promotes flexibility of the clock.
source: At the same time, the response of this splicing event to temperature promotes flexibility of the clock.
evidence: This is inferred from the temperature-dependent regulation of tim-tiny splicing.

claim: PER translation does not appear to be delayed relative to its mRNA production in a daily cycle.
source: In Drosophila, PER translation does not appear to be delayed relative to its mRNA production in a daily cycle (Chen et al., 1998), but the protein is initially destabilized through its phosphorylation by the DOUBLETIME (DBT) kinase (Price et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PER protein is initially destabilized through its phosphorylation by the DOUBLETIME (DBT) kinase.
source: In Drosophila, PER translation does not appear to be delayed relative to its mRNA production in a daily cycle (Chen et al., 1998), but the protein is initially destabilized through its phosphorylation by the DOUBLETIME (DBT) kinase (Price et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Alternative splicing has been implicated in the regulation of circadian clocks, but not previously linked to clock function in the manner reported in this study.
source: Although AS has been implicated in the regulation of circadian clocks, it has not been linked to clock function in the manner we report here.
evidence: This identifies the novelty of the current findings relative to previous work.

claim: In Neurospora crassa, the ratio of alternatively spliced frequency (frq) isoforms determines the robustness of circadian rhythmicity and fine-tunes the period length.
source: In Neurospora crassa, the ratio of alternatively spliced frequency (frq) isoforms determines the robustness of circadian rhythmicity and fine-tunes the period length (Garceau et al., 1997; Liu et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from other organisms, supported by citations.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, AS regulates the circadian clock by producing new isoforms that competitively inhibit functional clock proteins.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, AS regulates the circadian clock by multiple mechanisms, such as the production of new isoforms that competitively inhibit functional clock proteins (Seo et al., 2012) and the modulation of clock RNA levels via the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) pathway (James et al., 2012; Kwon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from other organisms, supported by citations.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, AS regulates the circadian clock by modulating clock RNA levels via the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) pathway.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, AS regulates the circadian clock by multiple mechanisms, such as the production of new isoforms that competitively inhibit functional clock proteins (Seo et al., 2012) and the modulation of clock RNA levels via the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) pathway (James et al., 2012; Kwon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from other organisms, supported by citations.

claim: In Drosophila, the alternative splicing regulator SR-related matrix protein of 160 kDa (SRm160) modulates PER levels locally in the pacemaker neurons to regulate circadian rhythms.
source: In Drosophila, the alternative splicing regulator SR-related matrix protein of 160 kDa (SRm160) modulates PER levels locally in the pacemaker neurons to regulate circadian rhythms (Beckwith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A key theme from studies on alternative splicing in circadian clocks is that AS acts directly on core clock components to set their levels.
source: The key theme that emerges from these studies is that AS acts directly on core clock components to set their levels.
evidence: This is a synthesis of knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Splicing mechanisms could regulate diurnal rhythmicity of neuronal excitability through splicing of BK channels in the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
source: Alternatively, splicing mechanisms could regulate diurnal rhythmicity of neuronal excitability, as proposed for splicing of BK channels in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (Shelley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: It is unlikely that the retention of tim-tiny leads to NMD-mediated RNA decrease because flies with prp4 downregulated do not have reduced tim levels.
source: It is unlikely that the retention of tim-tiny leads to NMD-mediated RNA decrease because the flies with prp4 downregulated do not have reduced tim levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tim RNA levels are not decreased.

claim: Overall tim RNA levels tend to be increased in flies with prp4 downregulated.
source: On the contrary, overall tim RNA levels tend to be increased in those flies.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of tim cDNA constructs with constitutively retained tim-tiny decreases TIM levels without altering tim mRNA levels.
source: Additionally, expression of tim cDNA constructs with constitutively retained tim-tiny (Figure 5) decreases TIM levels without altering tim mRNA levels (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by protein and RNA data from the cDNA expression experiments.

claim: It is either the tim mRNA translation step or the stability of the truncated TIM isoform (TIMtiny) that is sub-optimal when tim-tiny is retained.
source: Therefore, we suggest that it is either the tim mRNA translation step or the stability of the truncated TIM isoform, TIMtiny, produced by tim-tiny that is sub-optimal.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on the observed effects.

claim: The 267 amino acids at the C-terminus of TIM that are predicted to be lost in TIMtiny include a putative cytoplasmic localization signal.
source: The 267 amino acids at the C-terminus of TIM that are predicted to be lost in TIMtiny include a putative cytoplasmic localization signal (Saez et al., 2011) as well as a predicted threonine phosphorylation site (Bodenmiller et al., 2007), both of which could significantly change stability and function of TIM.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and cited literature.

claim: The 267 amino acids at the C-terminus of TIM that are predicted to be lost in TIMtiny include a predicted threonine phosphorylation site.
source: The 267 amino acids at the C-terminus of TIM that are predicted to be lost in TIMtiny include a putative cytoplasmic localization signal (Saez et al., 2011) as well as a predicted threonine phosphorylation site (Bodenmiller et al., 2007), both of which could significantly change stability and function of TIM.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and cited literature.

claim: Loss of the C-terminal 267 amino acids in TIMtiny could significantly change stability and function of TIM.
source: The 267 amino acids at the C-terminus of TIM that are predicted to be lost in TIMtiny include a putative cytoplasmic localization signal (Saez et al., 2011) as well as a predicted threonine phosphorylation site (Bodenmiller et al., 2007), both of which could significantly change stability and function of TIM.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional importance of the lost sequences.

claim: TIMtiny is typically not detected in western blots of TIM expression in flies.
source: Notably, TIMtiny is typically not detected in western blots of TIM expression in flies, so it appears that tim-tiny retention serves only to reduce the amount of tim RNA that can effectively produce protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data in the study.

claim: tim-tiny retention serves to reduce the amount of tim RNA that can effectively produce protein.
source: Notably, TIMtiny is typically not detected in western blots of TIM expression in flies, so it appears that tim-tiny retention serves only to reduce the amount of tim RNA that can effectively produce protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of detectable TIMtiny and the reduced full-length TIM.

claim: Cycles of tim-tiny and tim-cold intron retention are similar under light:dark and constant dark conditions.
source: Cycles of tim-tiny and tim-cold intron retention are similar under light:dark and constant dark conditions (Figure 6), but temperature cycles have different effects on the splicing of these two introns.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Temperature cycles have different effects on the splicing of tim-tiny and tim-cold introns.
source: Cycles of tim-tiny and tim-cold intron retention are similar under light:dark and constant dark conditions (Figure 6), but temperature cycles have different effects on the splicing of these two introns.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR splicing data in temperature cycles shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: tim-tiny intron is upstream of tim-cold.
source: tim-tiny intron is upstream of tim-cold, which means that tim-tiny retention should lead to TIM downregulation regardless of the splicing decision at the tim-cold locus.
evidence: This is based on the genomic positions of the introns shown in Figure 4B.

claim: tim-tiny retention should lead to TIM downregulation regardless of the splicing decision at the tim-cold locus.
source: tim-tiny intron is upstream of tim-cold, which means that tim-tiny retention should lead to TIM downregulation regardless of the splicing decision at the tim-cold locus.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential position of the introns.

claim: Following differential splicing at tim-tiny locus, tim-cold could get either retained or spliced, introducing an additional regulatory layer.
source: Following differential splicing at tim-tiny locus, tim-cold could get either retained or spliced, introducing an additional regulatory layer.
evidence: This is speculation about the combinatorial regulation of tim splicing.

claim: The interplay of AS at the level of tim-tiny and tim-cold introns can produce a range of TIM isoforms.
source: The interplay of AS at the level of these two introns can produce a range of TIM isoforms, the roles of which remain to be elucidated, particularly with respect to temperature entrainment.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple possible splicing outcomes.

claim: The roles of different TIM isoforms produced by alternative splicing remain to be elucidated, particularly with respect to temperature entrainment.
source: The interplay of AS at the level of these two introns can produce a range of TIM isoforms, the roles of which remain to be elucidated, particularly with respect to temperature entrainment.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge for future investigation.

claim: In Drosophila, splicing of D. melanogaster per intron 8 (dmip8) is regulated by both light and temperature.
source: In Drosophila, splicing of D. melanogaster per intron 8 (dmip8), the intron located in the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of per, is regulated by both light and temperature (Collins et al., 2004; Majercak et al., 2004; Majercak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: dmip8 splicing allows flies to delay their evening behavior during long photoperiods and/or high temperatures.
source: This splicing mechanism allows flies to delay their evening behavior during long photoperiods and/or high temperatures, and might play a role in seasonal adaptation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dmip8 function.

claim: dmip8 retention delays per mRNA and PER protein accumulation.
source: On a molecular level, dmip8 retention delays per mRNA and PER protein accumulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular effects of dmip8 splicing.

claim: dmip8 retention was not identified in the initial RNA-Seq data.
source: While dmip8 retention was not identified in our initial RNA-Seq data (Supplementary file 3 and 4), our follow up qPCR splicing analysis suggested that PRP4 modestly regulates per splicing (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Follow-up qPCR splicing analysis suggested that PRP4 modestly regulates per splicing.
source: While dmip8 retention was not identified in our initial RNA-Seq data (Supplementary file 3 and 4), our follow up qPCR splicing analysis suggested that PRP4 modestly regulates per splicing (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: dmip8 retention has a small effect on the free-running period length (~25 hr period).
source: dmip8 retention has a small effect on the free-running period length (~25 hr period) (Cheng et al., 1998; Majercak et al., 1999), but it cannot fully account for the period lengthening phenotype we report for flies with downregulated prp4 (Figure 1A–B; Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: dmip8 retention cannot fully account for the period lengthening phenotype in flies with downregulated prp4.
source: dmip8 retention has a small effect on the free-running period length (~25 hr period) (Cheng et al., 1998; Majercak et al., 1999), but it cannot fully account for the period lengthening phenotype we report for flies with downregulated prp4 (Figure 1A–B; Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the magnitude of effects.

claim: Studies in Arabidopsis suggest that the expression of a number of tri-snRNP components is regulated by the circadian clock.
source: Studies in Arabidopsis suggest that the expression of a number of tri-snRNP components is regulated by the circadian clock (Perez-Santángelo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from other organisms, supported by citation.

claim: Recent profiling of mRNA cycling in different neuronal clusters detected prp4 mRNA oscillations in DN1 clock neurons.
source: In Drosophila, recent profiling of mRNA cycling in different neuronal clusters detected prp4 mRNA oscillations in DN1 clock neurons and brr2 cycling in LNvs (Abruzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent profiling work.

claim: Recent profiling of mRNA cycling in different neuronal clusters detected brr2 cycling in LNvs.
source: In Drosophila, recent profiling of mRNA cycling in different neuronal clusters detected prp4 mRNA oscillations in DN1 clock neurons and brr2 cycling in LNvs (Abruzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent profiling work.

claim: Diurnal oscillations in tri-snRNP components may drive circadian splicing of tim and potentially other circadian output genes locally in specific clock neurons.
source: While these RNA-Seq findings have not been verified through other approaches, they lead us to hypothesize that diurnal oscillations in tri-snRNP components drive circadian splicing of tim (Figure 6) and potentially other circadian output genes locally in specific clock neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the cited RNA-Seq findings and the current study's data.

claim: A recent report suggests heterogeneous alternative splicing profiles for different circadian neuronal groups.
source: This hypothesis is further strengthened by another recent report (Wang et al., 2018) that suggests heterogeneous alternative splicing profiles for different circadian neuronal groups.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Circadian regulation of PRP4 kinase activity could contribute to differential splicing of tim over the course of the day.
source: In addition to changes in total levels of PRP4, circadian regulation of its kinase activity could contribute to differential splicing of tim over the course of the day.
evidence: This is speculation about an additional regulatory mechanism.

claim: PRP4 functions in LNvs, the key pacemaker cluster necessary for the maintenance of circadian cycles under constant dark conditions.
source: We establish a role for PRP4 in LNvs, the key pacemaker cluster necessary for the maintenance of circadian cycles under constant dark conditions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data from LNv-specific manipulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: PRP4 likely also functions in DN1s, clock cells implicated in temperature sensing and entrainment.
source: However, based on our findings that splicing of tim is regulated by temperature and persists in constant light (Figure 6), we speculate that PRP4 also functions in DN1s, clock cells implicated in temperature sensing and entrainment (Yadlapalli et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation based on the temperature regulation of tim splicing and cited literature on DN1 function.

claim: DN1s are clock cells implicated in temperature sensing and entrainment.
source: However, based on our findings that splicing of tim is regulated by temperature and persists in constant light (Figure 6), we speculate that PRP4 also functions in DN1s, clock cells implicated in temperature sensing and entrainment (Yadlapalli et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: Much of the focus in the circadian field has been on transcriptional or post-translational control.
source: In summary, while much of the focus in the circadian field has been on transcriptional or post-translational control, our findings indicate a critical role for alternative splicing, perhaps in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field.

claim: Alternative splicing plays a critical role in circadian regulation, perhaps in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: In summary, while much of the focus in the circadian field has been on transcriptional or post-translational control, our findings indicate a critical role for alternative splicing, perhaps in a cell-type-specific manner.
